extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, and students of composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for literary and expository style, emphasizing economy of reader attention, choice of words, figures, and the relation of authorial personality to form. Applies across genres from mathematical exposition to poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of attention
rubrics_metrics.description: All excellence of composition traces to the principle that a reader has a limited amount of attention; the relative goodness of two modes of expression may be determined by which requires the shortest process of thought for its comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer forms that minimize the cognitive effort required of the reader. An obscure style is one whose form 'obstructs his matter' by absorbing excessive attention; tedious language (monotony or redundancy) exhausts the reader's energies and diminishes understanding of the matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of the recipient's sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornaments of style (choice of words, figures, cadences, etc.) are devices that subserve the same purpose as economy of attention — they economize the recipient's sensibility and so increase force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat stylistic devices as instruments to conserve the reader's mental energy and to evoke associations that reduce explicit explanation. Use ornament when it helps the reader grasp or feel more with less explicit detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of fitting words (familiarity and brevity matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for Saxon (short, familiar) words is justified by their greater familiarity and brevity, which aids recognition and reduces effort; polysyllabic (Latin-derived) words can be used occasionally to suggest weightiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor familiar, brief words to speed recognition; reserve longer or rarer words when their effort signals importance or gravity. Word choice should serve ease of comprehension and the intended rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of figures of speech to economize attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of speech (metaphor, simile, tropes) are amenable to the law of economy — they allow a few words or images to call up many associated ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy metaphors and similes to suggest a network of associations rather than detailing everything; use them to compactly convey complex impressions. Avoid ornament that needlessly distracts rather than suggests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective imagery: choose particulars that imply many
rubrics_metrics.description: Select typical elements from a scene or sentiment which 'carry many others along with them' — by saying a few things but suggesting many, one abridges description and produces vivid impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer evocative particulars (illustrated by the Tennyson 'Mariana' extract) over exhaustive listing of facts. Anti-pattern: detailing every circumstance, which 'fritters' attention and weakens impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter and measured arrangement aid recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured movement (metre) in poetry gives pleasure due to the comparative ease with which metrically arranged words can be recognized, thus economizing attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize formal constraints (like metre) as aids to reader recognition and economy; use them intentionally to reduce decoding effort and enhance musical or mnemonic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortest process of thought as a canon of relative goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative goodness of any two modes of expressing an idea can be judged by observing which requires the shortest process of thought for comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing between alternative phrasings or structures, prefer the one that the reader can understand more directly and with less mental labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate style varies with subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Style must vary with its subject-matter: a perfect writer will adopt different modes (Junius, Lamb, Carlyle) depending on mood and topic; there is no one fixed style for all subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone, diction, and complexity to the topic and intended effect. Resist the notion that a single personal 'specific style' must dominate all writing contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid form obstructing matter (clarity over ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an author's form absorbs an inordinate amount of the reader's attention, it becomes an 'obscure style' that obstructs the matter; monotony and redundancy make prose tedious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity and the transmission of content over decorative or self-indulgent rhetorical flourishes that impede comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial personality increases linguistic complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the author's personality is involved, simpler language no longer suffices; as the author's personhood creeps into subject-matter, language becomes more complex in structure, word choice, and use of figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and permit greater stylistic complexity when subjective, individual perspective is integral to the material (e.g., in biography, history, poetry). In objective exposition, favor simpler, more dispassionate language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality and originality as merits of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is commonly accompanied by individuality of expression; marked originality in style often indicates an original mind — uniformity tends to mark mediocrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value distinctive voice and idiosyncratic traits when they genuinely reflect personal insight or power. Caveat: originality alone does not guarantee merit; it must serve substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance reader-centered and writer-centered perspectives on language
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's treatment isolates language in relation to the reader (objective view), but one must also consider devices of language as outcomes of the mind that employs them (writer-centered aspect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate style both for its effect on readers (economy of attention/sensibility) and as expressive of the writer's mind; consider unconscious traits as informative rather than dismissible noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and suggestiveness: maximize thought per word
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim 'to convey the greatest quantity of thoughts with the smallest quantity of words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice compression and suggestive phrasing so that a few well-chosen particulars evoke broader contexts; avoid verbose exposition when a compact image or phrase will suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate terminology and refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical and strictly objective discourse can be expressed simply and symbolically; scientific terminology is adequate when strictly adhered to; history, biography and poetry often require refined composition and subtler language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the level of terminological precision and rhetorical refinement appropriate to the genre: concise symbolic forms for algebra/math, disciplined scientific terms for expository science, and richer, more personal language for narrative and poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious linguistic traits reveal the author's self
rubrics_metrics.description: Tricks of diction, turns of thought, epithets, repetitions and phrases often reveal the speaker's personality unconsciously; such traits link the language to the mind that produced it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use awareness of unconscious stylistic markers for both self-reflection and critical evaluation: they can be evidence of authenticity and individuality, but may also betray affectation or weakness.
